caseno:
Civil Revision No. 700 of 1977 of 19 
From Misc. Appeal No. 24/1977
lawyer:
B.N. Chowdhury, Advocate with Parimal Chandra Guha, Advocate ------ For Petitioner. 
Sultan Ahmed, Deputy Attorney General ------ As Amicus curea.
parties:
Dilip Kumar Chakravorty ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Abdul Muyeed Chowdhury and Ors ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, J: This rule arises out of an application under section 115 (old) of the Code of Civil Procedure and is directed against an order passed by the Additional District Judge, Faridpur in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 24 of 1977 dated 13-4-77 reversing those passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Faridpur dated 21-1-1977 in Misc. Case No. 41 of 1976 passed under Order 39 Rule 2, Sub Rule (3) of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 2. The facts relevant for the purpose of this Rule are to the effect that the petitioner as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 141 of 1976 in the Court of the Munsif, Sadar, Faridpur against the opposite party, namely, the Deputy Commissioner, Faridpur and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.) Faridpur as principal defendants for permanent injunction restraining them from entering into the suit land, The petitioner also filed an application for temporary injunction for restraining the principal defendants from entering into the suit land till the disposal of the suit. The learned Munsif issued a show cause notice as also granted an ad-interim injunction on 5-2-76. Thereafter the suit was transferred on 16-3-76 to the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Faridpur under the order of the District Judge and the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 28 of 1976. The petitioner filed an application before the transferee court i.e. the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Faridpur under order 39, Rule 2 and 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging inter alia that the opposite parties violated and dis-obeyed the order of injunction granted by the learned Munsif on 18-8-1976 and by taking forcible possession of the suit properties. The said application was registered as Misc. Case No. 41 of 1976. Notices were sent to the opposite parties and the opposite parties in their written statement asserted that the order of ad-interim injunction was obtained against the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev.), as Custodian of vested and non-resident property and that the order of acquisition was for public purpose and made according to law. The learned Subordinate Judge after hearing the parties by his order dated 21-1-1977 found that there was a violation of the order of injunction by the defendant opposite parties and ordered that the moveable’s of the value of Tk. 500/- of the opposite parties be attached for violation of the order of injunction. It was also found by the learned Subordinate Judge that when there was an order of injunction there could not be any requisition of property before the injunction order is vacated. Against the said order, the opposite parties preferred an appeal and the learned Additional District Judge, Faridpur vacated the order passed by the learned Sub-Judge under order 39 rule 2 and 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure holding that the order of injunction passed by the Subordinate Judge was not in accordance with law in view of the fact that the Civil court had no jurisdiction to pass an order of injunction in view of the provisions of the East Pakistan Government and Local authority, Land and Building (Recovery of Possession) Ordinance 1970. In that view of the matter, the Additional District Judge held, the injunction itself having been passed unlawfully the question of violation does not arises. Against the said order and judgment of the learned Addl. District Judge the present Rule has been obtained. 

 3. The matter came up before a single Bench of this court but since a larger Bench should receive the question involved in the Rule, it has been referred to this Bench for a decision by the learned Chief justice. The petitioner was represented by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate. The opposite party did, not enter any appearance. The learned Deputy Attorney General (Civil) appeared to assist the court in the matter. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury has submitted that the order of the learned District Judge was not in accordance with law in view of, the tact that there was an order of injunction passed by the Court rightly or wrongly and until and unless the order is reversed the order remained in force and any violation of that order is liable to be punished in accordance with the provisions order 39 rule 2 and 3 of the Code of Civil procedure. The learned Deputy Attorney General only contended that the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is not in accordance with Order 39 rule 2 and 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure because of the fact that the court of learned Subordinate Judge has not issued the order of injunction as such the violation matter could not be heard by that court. It is only the issuing court which is competent to pass an order for violation of that order and no other court is competent to issue any order on breach of the order of injunction under order 39, Rule 1 C.P.C. He has cited certain Calcutta decisions, namely, A.I.R. 1914; Cal. 815; 61 C.L.J. 543, AIR .1962 Cal. 519 in support of his contention. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the petitioner on the other hand has referred to certain decisions reported in AIR 1962 Pat. 443; AIR 1923 Mad. 92; in support of his contention that the court which was in seisin of the case on transfer was competent to deal with the proceedings of violation of the order of injunction passed by the transferor court. The question in this rule is whether the words "Court granting the injunction" occurring in Rule 2(3) of order 39 of C.P.C. would mean that the Court which granted the injunction could alone punish the violation of the order of the injunction. This court has not pronounced any judgment on this question. But in India Calcutta High Court has taken a different view from that of Patna High Court, Punjab High Court and Allahabad High Court. The decisions of those courts have been referred to above. Mr. Sultan Ahmed, the learned Deputy Attorney General has referred to the aforesaid cases of Calcutta, High Court reported in 61 C.L.J. 543, AIR 1962 Cal. 519, AIR 1914 Cal. 815 in support of his contention. Sub-rule (3) of rule 2 of order 39 C.P. Code is to the following term:- 

 "(3) In case of disobedience or breach of any of the terms the Court granting the injunction may order the property of the person guilty of such disobedience or breach to be attached and may also order such.. person to be detained in the Civil prison for a term not exceeding six months unless in, the meantime the Court directs his release. 

 4. Mr. Sultan Ahmed the learned Deputy Attorney General has laid stress on the words the court granting the injunction occurring in the above sub-rule and argues that it is only the court which grants an order of injunction that can pass an order for violation of the order and no other court to which the case has been transferred subsequently can punish for violation of the order of injunction. The aforesaid cases of Calcutta High Court, cited by the learned Deputy Attorney General lay stress on the said words and the learned Judges in these decisions came to the finding that it is the court granting an order of injunction that only can punish not the Court to which the suit may subsequently be transferred. In the cases cited by Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the petitioner, it was held that the transferee court can also deal with the case of violation of the order of injunction passed by another court from which the case has been transferred to that Court. In the aforesaid cases referred to by the learned advocate for the petitioner, section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been referred to in deciding that the transferee court has under Order 39, Rule 2(3) of the C.P. C. has jurisdiction to punish in case of violation. Section 150 deals with the transfer of the business of the court and it has been held that in civil cases the transferee court has powers co-extensive with the transferor court. It has been argued that provisions of section 150 of Civil Procedure Code would apply where jurisdiction of one court is transferred to another court and does not apply to transfer of individual cases from one court to another. We are not concerned with that situation in the present case. Here, a case was transferred under section 24 of the C.P.C. from the court of the Munsif, Faridpur to that of Subordinate Judge, Faridpur. It was only a transfer of a single case to another court. Section 24 of the C.P.C. deals with the case of transfer and such transfer could be made by the High Court or the District Court at any stage either on an application of any of the parties after hearing them or on its own motion for trial or disposal to any other court subordinate to it and competent to dispose of the same in accordance with law. In a case of transfer of such nature U/S 24 the whole case is transferred and as such the transferee court has seision over the entire matter of the suit. If that be so, we do not understand why the transferee court cannot decide the question of violation of the order of injunction passed by the court from which the case has been transferred to that court. When a case is transferred from one court to another it means not only the transfer of the suit but the entire proceeding including the ancillary proceedings and hence all the matters are to be disposed of by the Transferee court. In the decisions reported in AIR 1968 Punjab (Hariana) page 374 it has been held to the following effect as under:— 

 "The transferee court should have powers co-extensive with the transferor court. Section 150 specifically provides that. But if transfer is of a particular case from the file of one court to another U/S 24, there is no reason under principle that the transferee court should not be held to have the same power as the court from which the case has been transferred. There seems to be no difference in principle. The disobedience of the order of the court under Or. 39, Rule 1, cannot be punished by the transferee court. Such will necessarily lead to bifurcation of the proceeding in the event of a transfer under section 24, transferor court in relation to the proceeding arising out of the order 39, Rule 1 and Rule 2(3) and the remaining proceedings in the suit to be conducted by the transferee court. In a conceivable case similar proceedings may have to be taken in the transferee court as well. Confusion will considerably be added if the suit had to be transferred again under section 24. The view which found favour with the High Courts of Patna and Allahabad appears to us to be inconsonance with the reason and the real intention of the legislature." 

 In that view of the matter, we are of the opinion that the transferee court to which the case is transferred under section 24 of the C.P.C. is competent to deal with the cases of breach of injunction and not to be confined with the court granting an injunction. In view of the matter our answer is that the court to which the case is transferred is also competent to deal with the case of the breach of injunction under sub-rule 3 of Rule 2 of Order 39 of Code of Civil Procedure. 

 7. The rule, therefore, is made absolute. The Judgment and order passed by the learned Additional District Judge is set aside and those passed by the learned Subordinate Judge is restored. In the facts and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.
